analysis.one_liner: Requires the President and Vice President to disclose tax returns and divest conflicting financial interests.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 23 Senate Democrats, was referred to committee in May 2023 and never received a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the President and Vice President to disclose their finances and recent tax returns within 30 days of taking office, and to sell or place in a blind trust any financial interest that could conflict with their official duties — including foreign payments barred by the Constitution's emoluments clause. It would also require major-party presidential candidates to release their tax returns, bar presidential appointees from working on matters involving the President's own interests, and let the Justice Department, state attorneys general, or aggrieved citizens go to court to enforce the rules. The bill never moved after being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The public, which gains visibility into whether the President and Vice President are personally profiting from the offices they hold. Federal employees and government contractors also benefit when appointees must step aside from matters involving the President's own financial interests.

how_it_helps.text: Presidents and Vice Presidents would have to disclose their financial interests and submit their three most recent tax returns — plus any returns under IRS audit — to Congress and the Office of Government Ethics within 30 days of taking office.

The President, Vice President, their spouses, and minor children would have to divest any financial interest that could pose a conflict of interest, either by selling it or moving it to a qualified blind trust — including interests that fall under the Constitution's ban on receiving payments from foreign governments.

Major-party presidential nominees would have to file their three most recent tax returns with the Federal Election Commission, where they would be made publicly available, and a sitting president would have to do the same within 30 days of the law taking effect.

Presidential appointees would be barred from working on any matter involving the President, the President's spouse, or entities in which they hold a substantial interest, with career officials taking over those matters instead.

The Justice Department, any state attorney general, or any aggrieved person could seek a court order if there is probable cause the President or Vice President has not complied with the divestiture rules.

analysis.who_pays: Presidents, Vice Presidents, and their families with outside business holdings, who would face public tax disclosure and be forced to sell or blind-trust conflicted assets — potentially at a moment of their choosing but under court scrutiny. Government officials close to the President would also recuse from some matters.

drawbacks.text: Forcing divestiture of an incumbent President's holdings raises legal questions the bill itself acknowledges: it includes a clause stating nothing in the act should be construed to violate the Constitution, reflecting arguments that some requirements on the presidency may face constitutional challenge.

Enforcement would run through the courts, where any 'person aggrieved' could sue to force divestiture — a broad standing provision that could produce years of litigation over a sitting president's assets.

The bill's statement that a violation would constitute an impeachable 'high crime or misdemeanor' is a sense of Congress with no binding legal force, and the divestiture standard still leaves the Office of Government Ethics wide discretion over what counts as conflict-free.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — forcing the nation's two highest officeholders to show their taxes and shed conflicted holdings — addresses a gap that became visible in practice when prior presidents held businesses while in office. The costs are real but narrow: litigation risk, divestiture friction, and unresolved constitutional questions. The main flaw is not design but the fact that it never got a hearing, so no version was ever tested or refined in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2023 and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which took no action on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on May 9, 2023, joined by 22 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting and future officeholders with outside financial interests, who avoided new tax disclosure and divestiture requirements, plus any businesses positioned to receive payments from a presidential family without public scrutiny.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without any floor action.

industries.industry: Presidential family businesses and private financial holdings
industries.note: The bill would force sitting Presidents and Vice Presidents to publicly disclose tax returns and sell or blind-trust any asset that could conflict with their official duties, ending the ability to keep operating a private business from the White House. It also bars their families from retaining foreign-government payments.

industries.industry: Foreign governments and foreign-owned entities seeking access to a sitting president
industries.note: Payments from kings, princes, or foreign-state-owned entities to the President or family would be treated as a conflict requiring divestiture, closing the channel for paid foreign favors.
